title: Turning Seawater into Fresh Water
summary: Long ago, people discovered a simple trick for turning salty sea water into fresh water, and today that same basic idea has grown into huge plants that supply dry places like Saudi Arabia and its Gulf neighbors with the water their people and farms depend on.
poll: Would you rather drink water that came from the sea or water that came from rain?

versions.title: Turning Seawater into Fresh Water
versions.text:
Look at the sea. It is big. It has lots of water. But we cannot drink it. It is too salty.

We need fresh water. Fresh water has no salt. We drink it. We use it on farms too.

Long ago, people found a trick. They put salty water in a pot. They made it hot. It turned to steam. The salt stayed in the pot. The steam went up. Then it got cool. It turned back to water. This new water had no salt in it!

This trick has a name. It is desalination. It means you take the salt out.

Today, big plants do this same trick. They turn sea water into fresh water. This helps dry lands.

Saudi Arabia is a dry land. It gets very little rain. Big plants there make fresh water from the sea. This water goes to homes. It goes to farms too. It helps so many people.

This clever trick got a name. It is called desalination. The word means taking the salt out of water.

Today, huge plants use this same trick. They turn salty sea water into clean fresh water. This helps dry lands that get little rain.

Saudi Arabia is one such dry land. It gets very little rain all year. Huge plants by the coast make fresh water from the sea. This water flows to homes and to farms. It helps millions of people every day.

versions.title: Turning Seawater into Fresh Water
versions.text:
Picture the vast ocean stretching toward the horizon, holding an almost unimaginable amount of water that looks inviting from a comfortable distance. Yet people cannot safely drink a single drop of it. Seawater contains far too much dissolved salt for the human body to process safely.

People need fresh water to survive. Fresh water contains little or no dissolved salt, which is exactly why we drink it constantly. Agriculture depends on it heavily too, to grow the food that eventually reaches our tables.

Long ago, resourceful people discovered a method for solving this exact problem using only simple tools. They boiled salty seawater inside a pot, and the water quickly turned into rising steam, leaving the dissolved salt behind at the bottom. That rising steam then touched a cooler surface nearby and condensed back into plain liquid water, carrying no trace of salt at all.

This process, called distillation, eventually gave rise to the modern science of desalination, meaning the removal of salt from water on an industrial scale. Engineers later improved on this basic idea again and again, searching for faster and cheaper ways to produce fresh water.

Today, enormous desalination plants use a related but far more advanced method called reverse osmosis. It pushes seawater through membranes containing microscopic pores too small for salt particles to pass through. These plants turn seemingly endless seawater into clean, drinkable fresh water around the clock, which especially helps arid regions receiving remarkably little rainfall each year.

One such notably arid region is Saudi Arabia and its Gulf neighbors, where rainfall remains scarce across the calendar year. This makes every drop of fresh water genuinely precious to daily life. Massive desalination plants along the coastline convert staggering amounts of seawater into usable fresh water daily, supplying homes, growing cities, and farms throughout the region and helping millions of people obtain water their lives depend on, a need that will likely keep growing as populations expand.

MID.modelAnswer: People use a method called desalination to turn sea water into fresh water. They boil salty sea water, and it rises as steam while the salt stays behind. The steam then cools and becomes plain, drinkable water with no salt left in it. This method matters greatly for dry regions, because places like Saudi Arabia and its Gulf neighbors get very little rain. Without this method, it would be much harder for people in those regions to survive and to grow the food they depend on.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how distillation and reverse osmosis are both solutions to the same problem, and why this matters especially for arid regions like Saudi Arabia and its Gulf neighbors. Use details from the passage.

Explains how reverse osmosis uses membranes to remove salt on a larger, more advanced scale
Connects both methods to the needs of arid regions with low rainfall
HIGH.modelAnswer: Distillation and reverse osmosis are both methods developed to solve the same basic problem: removing salt from seawater. Distillation, the older method, works by boiling seawater into steam, which leaves the dissolved salt behind, and then cooling that steam back into fresh liquid water. Reverse osmosis, a far more advanced and widely used method today, instead forces seawater through specialized membranes whose microscopic pores are too small for salt particles to pass through. Both methods matter enormously for arid regions like Saudi Arabia and its Gulf neighbors, where rainfall remains scarce all year, making desalination technology essential for supplying the fresh water that millions of people and their farms depend on.
